skyline.text: Amit Varma’s unwritten novel in which buildings break out in pustules
A hippie sleeps at the WHO gate, then fights smallpox
How protection came at last without killing the protected

brief.head: Weaken, wrap or build
brief.text: Vaccines are made by weakening a pathogen, by hiding its spike in a harmless carrier, or by building a lookalike molecule, Ajay Shah said. mRNA belongs to the last. {027-C09}

brief.head: America’s gift
brief.text: The US FDA is too conservative and slow, Ajay Shah said, but its published testing is a global public good. India should import from global manufacturers. {027-C11}

brief.head: Cheap, and nowhere
brief.text: Price caps meant to help the poor discourage producers and always create scarcity, Amit Varma said. A cheap vaccine you cannot find does you no good. {027-C07}

brief.head: Drowsier than drunk
brief.text: From Matthew Walker’s *Why We Sleep*, Amit Varma learnt that drivers short of sleep cause more accidents than drunk ones. Drunk driving is dangerous; sleepy driving more so. {027-R01}

brief.head: Influenza, misheard
brief.text: Ajay Shah once told Amit Varma to take the influenza vaccine. Varma heard “influencer”, and signed up at once: “You had me at hello.” {027-J02}

thought.text: A vaccine is first and foremost a private good.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, starting the case for vaccines from freedom rather than the state

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on vaccines and the state
lead.head: Love the jab, question the strap
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah are fans of vaccines. They are also fans of freedom. In India, Varma said, that is where things get “a little messy and complicated”.
Shah called the exercise “the toolkit in action”: the framework from their two previous episodes, on the state and on when it should act, applied to one question. {#toolkit}
First came the gushing. Something is injected into your body, perhaps in two or three shots, Shah said, and a disease is gone from your life. “Is this magical or what?”
He traced the story from pus-smeared inoculation through Edward Jenner’s cowpox to a Covid vaccine designed by software.
## Freedom first
Then Varma read out the popular case for the state: fund research, run the factories, ban imports, plan every jab and force the unwilling. “I think they’re all rubbish,” he said.
Shah answered from first principles. Freedom is the default, so begin with no state at all and ask what, if anything, fails.
“A vaccine is first and foremost a private good,” he said. The person who gets it benefits most, as with eating a chocolate or getting a toothache fixed. {027-C01}

There is a market failure: your vaccination also protects the people around you, a positive externality. But it bites only for those who will not pay. Anyone who buys a vaccine out of self-interest is done.

Unlike education, where everyone underinvests, a vaccine is a yes-or-no decision. “Vaccines are only integer valued,” Shah said. “They’re the zero or they’re one. For the ones, it’s game over.” {027-C03}
For the zeros, the answer is a voucher: the state tops up what a person would pay. That justifies funding, Shah said, not state factories, import bans or central planning.
## The strap question
Eradication is different. The common cold moves among many species, including pigs, and rabies survives in dogs and foxes. But smallpox and polio live only in humans, so they can be wiped out.
A world without smallpox, Shah argued, is a true public good: nobody’s share of it diminishes anyone else’s, and no newborn can be shut out. {027-C04}
That raised a moral puzzle. A state that touches your body, Shah said, ranks with the death penalty, torture and incarceration in intrusiveness. What of conscientious objectors?
For eradication alone, Shah would sign up for significant coercion, though each listener must decide. Varma, cast as the man strapped down, protested: “You really want to strap me down, don’t you?”
Varma set his own bar. The coercion he cheers today, he argued, could tomorrow be used for something he opposes. Where forcing happens, “the bar should be very high.” {027-C06}
Shah added a darker thought: future biotechnology might give governments vaccines that “make a population more docile, more controllable”.
## Roll up your sleeve

The episode closed with a prescription. Shah wants vaccines counted among everyday health-seeking behaviours, with sleep hygiene, nutrition and exercise, and adults to take the whole array made for them.
“Vaccines are not a zone of government,” he said. “They should be a zone of the people.” Post them on Instagram, he urged, and give your friends FOMO.
Varma, who got Covishield the very day he could, promised to take many of the vaccines Shah recommends.

second.label: The mRNA miracle
second.head: File in, vaccine out
second.deck: Ajay Shah on the day software designed a Covid vaccine
body: When Covid broke out, Amit Varma recalled, some experts predicted we might never find a vaccine. {#never} Vaccines had traditionally taken years, if not decades, and the search for an HIV vaccine still goes on.
Instead, Ajay Shah said, “some folks in China sequenced the SARS-CoV-2 and uploaded a file. Then a piece of software read that file and printed out the design of the mRNA vaccine.” {027-S03}

All the remaining delay, Shah said, came from testing by the US FDA and from building factories to scale up. The design itself, Varma noted, came practically the same day the virus was sequenced and put online.

quote.text: Just pause to think of the madness of what was said

second.caption: the vaccine designed by software

third.head: How the wheels came off
body: Before the show, a shortlist. Amit Varma said the hosts brainstormed for a long time, not about content but about a name. Two made the final: *Watching the Wheels* and *Everything is Everything*.
The first is John Lennon’s song, which Ajay Shah called contemplative and humble: the universe trundles along while we watch “with an air of amusement”. {#lennon} Everyone would know it.

The second is a line from Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*, on *The Rising*, the album he wrote after the 9/11 attacks. Shah said: “So it’s like my world is here, everything is there, but you are missing.” {027-S05}
Tested on many people, the second won. Lennon still opens the episode: the hosts’ young friend Ishaan Chintamani sang *Watching the Wheels* for them, with his father Gaurav on guitar. {#ishaan}

p2.title: Needles and liberty
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah put their framework for state action to work on vaccines {#toolkit}

sections.label: The marvel
sections.head: Better than the moon
sections.caption: the miracle of vaccines
body: “I love vaccines,” Ajay Shah said. “Vaccines are the greatest thing. It’s like as cool as going to the moon and back.” {#moon}
Shah said he is grateful to the universe for having made so many vaccines, to match all the pathogens Mother Nature left wandering around the planet trying to get their teeth into us.
Their ancestors were crude. Inoculators smeared smallpox pus into cuts; Edward Jenner found that cowpox protected without killing. Modern vaccines, Shah said, come in three kinds.
## Three recipes
Attenuated vaccines take a pure culture of the pathogen and damage it, with heat, acid or other techniques, leaving enough for the immune system to learn from.

Engineered carriers are the second route. The AstraZeneca vaccine, sold in India as Covishield, places the SARS-CoV-2 spike inside a chimpanzee virus harmless to humans, and injects something like a trillion particles. {#trillion} The immune system learns the protein surface of the spike, so the body is ready when the real virus shows up.

Synthetic vaccines construct a novel molecule that looks like the virus, and mRNA belongs here. Shah said he was not the right person to explain it, but called it “a pinnacle of human knowledge of biology”.

~ A manufactured vaccine carries no risk of getting sick, he said, whereas some attenuated vaccines make one person in ten thousand ill. Very high efficacy, often near-zero side effects: to Shah, all of it is a miracle. {027-C09}

quote.text: mRNA is absolutely magical. It’s a miracle of modern science. It’s one of the greatest achievements.

sections.label: The first test
sections.head: Zero, one, game over
sections.caption: vaccines as a private good
body: Amit Varma listed the popular wisdom: the state should fund research, run factories, ban imports, plan every jab and coerce refusers. Whisper “committee, budget” in a bureaucrat’s ear at bedtime, he said, and “they’ll go to sleep with a beatific smile on their face”. {027-J01}
Ajay Shah began where the toolkit begins. Freedom is the default: imagine no state at all, then ask what, if anything, fails.
The answer starts with self-interest. Get vaccinated and you are protected, as surely as you get utility from a chocolate. “A vaccine is first and foremost a private good,” Shah said. {027-C01}
The market failure is a positive externality. In a studio where Shah gabs “at high speed”, his vaccination protects Varma too. But it matters only for those who decline to pay. {027-C02}
## Taken or not
That sets vaccines apart from education, where every single person underinvests, so the failure is universal. A vaccine is taken or not taken. “For the ones, it’s game over.” {027-C03}
For the zeros, the standard fix is a voucher: the state tops up a person’s own willingness to pay, to reflect the gain to everyone else.
~ For a frightening enough disease, people will buy vaccines unprompted; for flu there are shades of grey. Either way, Shah said, an externality motivates funding, not the rest of Varma’s list.

quote.text: Then actually, for me, the story is over, there is no market failure.

sections.label: The high bar
sections.head: Wiped out, and good for all
sections.caption: eradication and the body
body: Some diseases can never be beaten. The common cold moves in and out of many species, including pigs, Ajay Shah said, and rabies has a reservoir in dogs and foxes. You simply make do.
A few pathogens, such as smallpox and polio, live only in humans. Get the vaccine to every person in the world and the horror is gone forever.

Such a world, Shah argued, is a public good. The show’s young camera crew, Vaishnav and Nomsita, never had a smallpox vaccine; only “old people like me” had. No one’s enjoyment of a smallpox-free world diminishes another’s, and no newborn can be excluded. {027-C04}
## Hands off the body
Then came the puzzle. A state that touches your body, Shah said, sits with the death penalty, torture and incarceration on the scale of intrusion. {027-C05}

What of a few thousand conscientious objectors who refuse a smallpox vaccine on religious grounds? Shah pictured officials strapping down “Amit Bhai” as he hollered and screamed, “a scene straight out of *One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest*”. Varma asked which Amit Bhai he meant. {027-J04}
~ Shah’s answer: for smallpox or polio eradication, he would sign on for significant coercion. But he called himself “a tiny irrelevant person”. Each of us, he said, must make our own choice.

quote.text: Eradication projects and only eradication projects have the high bar of public goods.

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Coercion, the other epidemic
sections.caption: consent and coercion
body: Amit Varma calls himself “a huge pro vaccine” person; he got vaccinated against Covid the very day it was possible. {#covishield} He is also, he said, “a huge pro freedom person”, and to him consent matters.

Should a good thing be forced on people? The coercion he favours today, Varma argued, might tomorrow be used for something he opposes. The question is whether the forcing itself is good, and the bar should be very high. {027-C06}
Coercion, he said, is a social ill, and “a more endemic disease than any other”.
Ajay Shah offered a reason for caution. Future biological technology, he said, might let governments use vaccines “that make a population more docile, more controllable”. {#docile}
## Cloaked in kindness
Varma named two coercions with good intentions and bad outcomes. The first is price controls, which discourage producers and innovators and hurt the poor more than they help. {027-C07}

The second is a state monopoly on supply, which only slows vaccination. Let the government run its programme, Varma said, but let private players in too. When richer people pay “a bomb” for an mRNA vaccine, scarce cheap supply is freed for those who cannot afford it. {027-C08}
~ Shah’s only doubt was about the good intentions. “I’m not even sure about the intentions,” he said.

quote.text: And price controls always lead to scarcities. All it means is you won’t get the damn thing.

sections.label: The prescription
sections.head: Show off your shots
sections.caption: adult vaccines
body: Amit Varma described himself as “like a little boy bubbling with joy”. Tell him chocolates are good, and he wants chocolates. Tell him vaccines are good: “I want vaccines.”

Ajay Shah wants vaccines enshrined as a first-class part of health-seeking behaviour, alongside sleep hygiene, nutrition and exercise. Many of us think vaccines are for children, or are something the government does. Both propositions, he said, are wrong.
“Vaccines are not a zone of government,” he said. “They should be a zone of the people.” Tell your friends you finished your third dose. Put the picture on Instagram. Create FOMO. {027-C10}
## A free lunch

Shah pointed readers to the US CDC’s list of adult vaccines, approved by the US FDA, and its schedule by age, showing which need a new shot every year or every three years. The list runs to 18 vaccines. {#eighteen}

He thinks the FDA too conservative and too slow. That makes its approval a high bar, and its published testing a global public good. India and Bangladesh, he said, should import from global manufacturers. {027-C11}
The hosts’ friend Rajeshwari Sengupta paid for 42 vaccines for her child. {#fortytwo}
~ Paying up front to rule out disease is, to Shah, “just a free lunch”. Prevention is better than cure.

quote.text: So something being approved by the US FDA is a high bar.

side.boxText: Episodes 25 and 26, *Understanding the State* and *When Should the State Act?*, built a general method for public policy: freedom is the default, so hunt first for market failures. This episode, Ajay Shah said, is a demo of it. {#demo}

contQuote.text: But tomorrow it might be something I’m not in favour of, which is being forced upon me. So we should go to the principle itself. Is the forcing good? Is the forcing bad?

p3.title: Tales of the pox
p3.deck: Pus, cows, a guru’s dream and a city that falls ill

stories.start: One of the greatest uh Indian stories is the journey of the eradication
stories.end: a dream that can actually have some vast consequences for the world
stories.caption: Larry Brilliant and the goddess’s dream
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a hippie, a guru and India’s smallpox fight
stories.head: Sent down the hill by a goddess
body: In the early 1970s, Ajay Shah said, smallpox had been eradicated through most of the world. India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Somalia were the last holdouts, a reservoir from which the disease could one day bounce back. {#holdouts}
Among the colourful characters in the fight was Larry Brilliant, a hippie living with a Hindu spiritual guide in the Himalayas. Shah forgot the guru’s name; Amit Varma supplied it: Neem Karoli Baba.
One day the Baba said a goddess had told him in a dream that Larry must go down to the plains and conquer smallpox. Larry was baffled: what could he do? The Baba ordered him out.

Larry left the ashram near Rishikesh and took the overnight bus. At 4 a.m. he reached the WHO compound in Delhi. {#fouram} Nobody was there; some dogs were barking. With nowhere else to go, he slept at the gate.

In the morning, people came and wondered who he was. He had a degree in medicine, so they signed him on as a junior flunky in the smallpox programme. “He was brilliant,” Shah said. “He was very brilliant.” {027-J05}
One thing led to another, and Larry Brilliant ended up as one of the top people who led India’s smallpox eradication programme. {027-S04}
~ Varma, for his part, had another theory about the dream: perhaps Larry had not bathed for three days, and the Baba made up the goddess to be rid of him. “Enough is enough,” said Shah. {027-J06}
stories.why: One of the great public-health triumphs in India turned partly on chance: a guru’s dream, an overnight bus and a hippie asleep at a gate. Small, odd events, the story shows, can have vast consequences for the world.
stories.postscript: Shah loves the smallpox story so much, he said, that he could not resist telling it: “a triumph of human achievement”.

stories.start: a quick story of vaccination. Vaccination started a long time ago as inoculation
stories.end: in terms of the capacity for the inoculation to kill the person
stories.caption: inoculation
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the gruesome ancestor of the vaccine
stories.head: A little pus, a lot of nerve
body: Smallpox killed a quarter of the children who caught it, Ajay Shah said, and over the first ten or twenty years of life almost everyone met it. {#quarter}

The answer was mild exposure. Inoculators broke a pustule on an infected person, cut a healthy child’s skin and smeared in the white pus. “Does that sound suitably disgusting and gross and scary as hell?” Shah asked. {027-S01}

About one in ten inoculated children still caught smallpox and died. But 10 per cent beats 25. Shah said there is fair evidence the practice began in India, though perhaps in the Ottoman Empire; it likely travelled on to Europe’s imperial courts.
~ The trouble was the dose. Smallpox is so virulent, Shah said, that a tenth or a hundredth as much pus probably made little difference to the risk. {#dose}
stories.why: People understood the principle of immunity long before they understood the biology. Without a way to control the dose, though, protection came at a terrible price, and the next leap would be keeping the protection without the killing.

stories.start: The next revolution came from cowpox, where Edward Jenner observed that the women
stories.end: Okay, this led to the whole modern idea around vaccines
stories.caption: Edward Jenner and cowpox
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the relative that protected against smallpox
stories.head: Cowpox to the rescue
body: Edward Jenner noticed that the women who worked with cows often caught cowpox, a relative of smallpox. Once they had it, Ajay Shah said, they were completely immunised against smallpox.
This was seriously great, Shah said, because cowpox does not kill at a 10 per cent probability, as inoculation did. It is a minor disease. {#cowpox}
The trick lay in the gap. Cowpox is different enough from smallpox not to kill you, and close enough to deliver protection. It was, Shah said, a huge leap in thinking. {027-S02}
~ Inoculators already knew that exposure protects. Jenner’s idea, Shah said, was protection “without killing a large fraction of the people”, and from it grew the whole modern idea of vaccines.

quote.text: That was a huge intellectual breakthrough by Edward Jenner.

stories.start: my smallpox story is not even a smallpox story. It's a work of fiction
stories.end: suddenly at one point you said I have a story that I remembered this
stories.caption: Smallpox Town
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a surreal novel he never wrote
stories.head: The city that caught smallpox
body: In his early twenties, Amit Varma read a great book on smallpox, whose name he has forgotten, and a detailed *New Yorker* essay.
They gave him an idea for a novel called *Smallpox Town*, written as one word. “And in that a city get smallpox. Not the people in the city. The city gets smallpox.” {027-S06}

The buildings would break out in pustules and the ground would scab over. Whatever happens in the course of the disease would happen not to the people but to the city: “sufficiently dystopian and surreal”, he said.

~ He was young, and forgot the idea, until Ajay Shah’s smallpox story brought it back. He confessed he had not read Albert Camus’s *The Plague*, though he had read *L’Etranger*, and recited its opening: “my mother died today, or was it yesterday”. {027-J11}
stories.why: Reading non-fiction about a disease can spark surreal fiction. And an idea forgotten since one’s early twenties can resurface years later, when a friend’s story about the same disease touches the right nerve.

quiz.q: What did early inoculators smear into a cut on a healthy child’s skin?
quiz.a: White pus from a broken pustule on someone sick with smallpox.

quiz.q: Why did women who worked with cows escape smallpox, as Edward Jenner noticed?
quiz.a: They caught cowpox, a mild relative, which left them immune to smallpox.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah call vaccines ‘integer valued’, unlike spending on education?
quiz.a: You take it or you don’t, and for takers there is no market failure.

quiz.q: Why can smallpox and polio be eradicated, but never rabies or the common cold?
quiz.a: Smallpox and polio live only in humans; the others have animal reservoirs.

quiz.q: Who ordered Larry Brilliant down to the plains to fight smallpox, and why?
quiz.a: Neem Karoli Baba, who said a goddess had told him so in a dream.

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma learn about drivers from Matthew Walker’s *Why We Sleep*?
quiz.a: Drivers short of sleep cause more accidents than drivers who are drunk.
